title: Ninety-Seven of 104 World Cup Matches Face Significant Heat Risk: What Fans Travelling From India Need to Know
excerpt: Climate scientists warn that the 2026 FIFA World Cup across the US, Mexico, and Canada could be the hottest major sporting event in history — and millions of South Asian fans heading to stadiums need a survival plan
body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicked off this week with Mexico's 2-0 victory over South Africa in front of a roaring crowd at the Estadio Azteca. But behind the spectacle of the biggest World Cup in history — 48 teams, 104 matches, 16 venues across three countries — climate scientists are raising an alarm that has nothing to do with tactics or VAR controversy. The tournament, they say, is on a collision course with extreme heat.

Two major scientific analyses published in the lead-up to the tournament paint a concerning picture. A study by World Weather Attribution and the Climate Central research group found that 97 of the 104 scheduled matches face "significant heat risk," with 26 matches projected to take place at wet-bulb globe temperatures (WBGT) of 26°C or above — the threshold at which athletic performance degrades and heat illness risk rises sharply. Five matches, all in the southern US and Mexico, are expected to hit WBGT levels of 28°C or higher, classified as "dangerous" by international sports medicine standards.

## Why This World Cup Is Different

Previous summer World Cups in hot climates — South Korea and Japan in 2002, Brazil in 2014 — dealt with heat, but the 2026 edition faces a unique convergence of factors. The tournament runs from June 11 to July 19, spanning peak summer across a vast geographic range. Venues include cities like Dallas, Houston, and Atlanta, where June and July temperatures routinely exceed 35°C (95°F), with humidity levels that push the heat index far higher.

Of the 16 stadiums hosting matches, only three have air conditioning: AT&T Stadium in Arlington (Dallas), NRG Stadium in Houston, and Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta — all retractable-roof venues that can seal in cooled air. The remaining 13, including MetLife Stadium in New Jersey (which hosts the final), SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, and Lumen Field in Seattle, are either open-air or partially enclosed.

"The sheer number of matches at dangerous heat levels is unprecedented for a FIFA tournament," said Theodore Keeping, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who contributed to the World Weather Attribution study. "And this is with current climate projections — a single heatwave event during the tournament could push conditions well beyond what models predict."

## FIFA's Response: Hydration Breaks and Monitoring

FIFA has mandated three-minute cooling breaks in each half of every match when WBGT exceeds 25°C. Medical teams at each venue will continuously monitor conditions, with authority to extend breaks or, in extreme cases, suspend play.

Professor Chris Minson, an exercise physiologist at the University of Oregon who has advised Olympic and FIFA medical committees, noted that the hydration breaks are a meaningful step. "Three minutes doesn't sound like much, but it allows core temperature to begin dropping and gives players access to ice towels and cold fluids. The data from the Tokyo Olympics showed these interventions measurably reduce heat casualty rates."

Dr Julien Périard, a heat physiology expert at University College London, added a critical nuance: "The breaks help players, but fans in the stands don't get the same relief. In open-air stadiums with direct sun exposure, spectators can be at higher risk than athletes because they're not acclimatised and they're often dehydrated."

## What NRI Fans Need to Know

For the estimated two to three million South Asian-origin fans expected to attend at least one World Cup match — whether driving from Houston, flying from the Bay Area, or visiting from India — the heat risk is real and requires planning.

**Before the match:**

Acclimatisation matters. If you are flying in from a cooler region or from India's monsoon season (where humidity is high but direct sun exposure patterns differ), arrive at least a day early and spend time outdoors to adjust. Pre-hydrate with electrolyte-rich fluids — not just water — starting 24 hours before the event. Nimbu pani with a pinch of salt is effective and familiar.

**At the stadium:**

Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting clothing. A broad-brimmed hat or umbrella is essential — many venues allow personal sun umbrellas. Apply SPF 50+ sunscreen and reapply every two hours. Avoid alcohol before and during the match; it accelerates dehydration.

FIFA's official fan zones and stadiums will have water stations, but lines can be long. Bring a sealed, empty water bottle (most venues allow these through security) and fill it inside.

**Know the warning signs:**

Heat exhaustion presents as heavy sweating, nausea, dizziness, headache, and rapid pulse. If you or someone near you shows these symptoms, move to shade, apply cool water, and seek medical attention. Heat stroke — marked by confusion, hot dry skin, and loss of consciousness — is a medical emergency requiring immediate help.

**High-risk matches for Indian-origin fans:**

Matches in Dallas (AT&T Stadium) and Houston (NRG Stadium) are in air-conditioned venues and are the safest bets for comfort. Matches at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey and Gillette Stadium near Boston carry lower heat risk due to coastal proximity but can still surprise with summer humidity spikes. The most challenging conditions are expected at matches in Mexico City's Estadio Azteca (altitude plus heat) and any late-afternoon kickoffs in the southern US.

## A Broader Climate Reckoning

The heat risk at the 2026 World Cup is not an anomaly — it is a preview of what global sport faces as temperatures continue to rise. The 2022 World Cup in Qatar was moved to November specifically to avoid lethal summer conditions. The 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles and the 2034 World Cup awarded to Saudi Arabia will face even more extreme challenges.

For the millions of Indian-origin fans across North America who see this World Cup as a once-in-a-generation celebration, the message is not to stay home — it is to go prepared. Pack the sunscreen alongside the vuvuzela, bring the electrolytes with the flags, and treat the heat as seriously as you would the altitude at a Himalayan trek.

The beautiful game deserves to be watched in comfort, not endured in distress.

*Sources: World Weather Attribution study, Climate Central analysis, Scientific American, Reuters Climate Monitor, Le Monde, interviews with Theodore Keeping (Imperial College London), Chris Minson (University of Oregon), Julien Périard (UCL)*
